Indikator 10c tracks the 30-day mortality rate for patients with a Charlson Score of 3 or higher, providing a critical measure of healthcare outcomes across Danish regions and hospitals. For the 2022/23 analysis period, the data reveals significant variation in mortality rates and a universal failure to meet the established clinical standard [^src1]. Not a single region or hospital fulfilled the standard, with the fulfillment rate sitting at 0% across all measured entities [^src1].

The highest mortality rates were recorded at Regionshospitalet Horsens and Rigshospitalet, both reporting a rate of 33.3% [^src1]. Hospitalerne i Nordsjælland also reported a high rate of 28.8% [^src1]. On the other end of the spectrum, the lowest mortality rate was observed at Regionshospitalet Randers at 6.7%, followed by Bispebjerg og Frederiksberg Hospitaler at 10.9% and Sygehus Lillebælt at 12.0% [^src1]. The national average for Denmark stood at 20.3% [^src1].

Historical data included in the table highlights substantial volatility and diverging trends over the past three years. Regionshospitalet Randers demonstrated a dramatic improvement, with its mortality rate plummeting from 52.2% in 2020/21 to 24.0% in 2021/22, and finally to 6.7% in 2022/23 [^src1]. In contrast, Hospitalerne i Nordsjælland experienced a concerning upward trend, rising from 10.5% in 2020/21 to 24.6% in 2021/22, and reaching 28.8% in 2022/23 [^src1]. At the national level, the overall mortality rate improved from 23.1% in 2020/21 to 19.6% in 2021/22, before ticking up slightly to 20.3% in 2022/23 [^src1].

Several outliers in the dataset warrant caution regarding statistical reliability. Both Bornholms Hospital and Regionshospitalet Randers have their exact patient counts suppressed (marked as #/#), indicating small sample sizes [^src1]. This low volume likely explains the extreme year-over-year percentage swings seen at these facilities, such as Bornholms Hospital dropping from 42.9% to 0.0% before rebounding to 28.6% [^src1].
